questions.question: For real numbers $x$ and $y$, what does trichotomy say?
options: All three of $x \lt y$, $x = y$, and $x \gt y$ may be true.
Exactly one of $x \lt y$, $x = y$, or $x \gt y$ is true.
At least two of $x \lt y$, $x = y$, and $x \gt y$ must be true.
No comparison between real numbers is possible.

questions.question: What does trichotomy imply about the ordering of real numbers?
options: Every pair of real numbers is equal.
Comparisons between real numbers are decisive.

questions.question: Which one of the three trichotomy alternatives is true for $2$ and $5$?
For the real number $x = -3$, which sign case from the equivalent formulation holds?
Why is the word exactly important in the trichotomy proposition?
options: It means at least one alternative holds, but several may hold together.
It means one and only one of the three alternatives holds.
It means the alternatives are optional.
It means equality is excluded from real numbers.

questions.question: How is trichotomy used in many proofs?
options: By replacing real numbers with complex numbers.
By proving all real numbers are zero.

questions.question: If $x$ and $y$ are real numbers and $x\ \neq y$, what follows from trichotomy?
Suppose $x$ is a real number and $x$ is not zero and not positive. Which case must hold?
Which statement correctly identifies the scope of the proposition?
options: It is stated for all complex numbers.
It is stated only for natural numbers written as $n$.
It is stated for real numbers.
It is stated only for functions.

questions.question: Real numbers satisfy trichotomy: exactly one of $x<0$, $x=0$, $x>0$ holds. Why does this fail for $\mathbb{C}$?
options: They satisfy exactly the same order trichotomy as real numbers.
They do not have this trichotomy property as stated for real numbers.

questions.question: A proof considers real numbers $x$ and $y$ and splits into $x \lt y$, $x = y$, and $x \gt y$. Which principle justifies that these cases cover all possibilities without overlap?
If $x,y\in\mathbb{R}$ and someone claims both $x \lt y$ and $x = y$, what does trichotomy say?
options: The claim is impossible; exactly one relation holds
The claim is possible for all real numbers
The claim is possible only when $x = 0$.

questions.question: For real numbers $x$ and $y$, how many of $x \lt y$, $x=y$, and $x \gt y$ can hold?
What are the three sign cases for a real number $x$?
What does trichotomy express about real-number order?
options: Every real number is an integer.

questions.question: Which relation is true for $-3$ and $-1$?
Suppose $x\in\mathbb{R}$ is not zero and not negative. What must be true?
For real numbers $a$ and $b$, which list gives the complete trichotomy cases?
Why are the three trichotomy cases useful in proofs?
options: They prove every number is zero.
They apply only to unordered sets
